title: How to Write a Sermon, From Blank Page to Pulpit
subtitle: A complete repeatable method for writing a sermon, from first reading of the text to a finished message you can preach with conviction on Sunday.

sections.title: Four Days Out and Nothing
sections.body:
It is Wednesday. Sunday is coming whether you are ready or not.

The blank page is the same every week, and every week it tells you the same lie, that you have nothing, that the well is dry, that this is the one that finally exposes you. Most preachers do not have a writing problem. They have a process problem. They sit down to write a sermon when they have not yet done the work that makes writing possible, and so the panic is not a failure of talent. It is a failure of sequence.

A repeatable method will not make you a great preacher. But it will get you to Sunday with something true in your hands, week after week, year after year, when inspiration does not show up. And inspiration mostly does not show up. The men who preach well for decades are not waiting on lightning. They are running a process they trust, and the process carries them through the dry weeks when nothing in them wants to climb into a pulpit at all.

sections.title: First, Live in the Text
sections.body:
Before you write a word, you read. And then you read again.

Start Monday, not Friday. Take the passage and read it slowly, out loud, more than once. Read it in a couple of translations. Read what comes before it and after it, because no paragraph stands alone. Do not reach for commentaries yet. Sit in the text first, with a pen, and write down everything you notice, every question, every word that snags, every repetition, every turn. Most of what you notice will not make the sermon. But you cannot preach what you have not seen.

Then do the labor. What did this mean to the people who first heard it. Where does it sit in the book. What is the author doing, not just saying. Now bring in the scholars, the commentaries, the lexicons, the men who have spent their lives in this text, and let them correct you and deepen you. Take your own observations to them, not their conclusions to your sermon. The goal of these first two days is one sentence you do not yet have. The main point of the passage. Not your point. Its point. You are not ready to write until you can say what the text is about in a single clear line.

sections.title: Find the Spine and the Aim
sections.body:
A sermon is not a pile of true things. It is one thing, said well, that goes somewhere.

Once you have the point of the text, write two sentences and do not skip this. First, what is this sermon about, in one line, the big idea. Second, what should happen in the people who hear it, the aim. Not what they will know. What will change. A man who cannot say where his sermon is going will wander, and his people will wander with him, and they will all arrive nowhere together.

Now build the spine. Let the structure come from the text, not from a template. If the passage is an argument, follow the argument. If it is a story, follow the story. If it has three movements, you may have three movements. Do not force three points onto a text that has two, or one. The outline serves the text. The text does not serve your outline. By the end of day three you should have a single big idea, a clear aim, and a skeleton drawn from the passage itself. The flesh comes next. The bones come first.

sections.title: Write It the Way You Speak
sections.body:
Now you write. And here is the rule most preachers break. Write for the ear, not the eye.

A sermon is spoken. The sentence that looks elegant on the page can strangle a man in the pulpit. Write the way you talk when you are gripped by something true, short sentences, plain words, room to breathe. Fill in the spine. Take the hardest point and make it land with an image, a case, a face from your week. Build each section toward its point and let the point be sharp.

Watch the proportions. Most sermons spend too long getting started and too little time on the text and the turn. Cut the throat-clearing. Get to the passage. And do the work of moving from what the text says to what it asks of this room, the actual Tuesday, the actual fear, the actual sin in the third pew. Do not end on be nicer and try harder. Run every demand through the gospel, what God has done before what you must do.

Write the whole thing if that is how you think. Then you can decide what to carry into the pulpit. But write it. The discipline of finishing the sentence is the discipline that makes a preacher.

sections.title: Preach It to Yourself First
sections.body:
The sermon is not finished when the manuscript is finished. It is finished when it has gone through you.

Read it out loud, on your feet, before you ever stand before the church. You will hear what is dead. You will hear the sentence that runs too long, the point that does not land, the section you love that does the sermon no good. Cut it. The line you are most proud of is often the line that has to go, because it serves you and not the text.

Then do the harder thing. Let the sermon preach to you. Sit under it. Ask whether the word you are about to bring to them has done anything to you this week, whether you are inside the indictment or pointing from a safe distance. A man who has not been moved by his own sermon will not move anyone, and the people can tell. They always can.

The method gets you to Sunday with something true. The prayer that follows the method gets you to Sunday with something alive. Do all the work. Refuse the laziness that calls itself trusting God. And then kneel, because the work cannot do the one thing only God can do, and the blank page was never the real problem. The real problem was always whether you would let the text have you first.
